fixes.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].
fixes.why: only 2 marks; marked 'governs' from sir's vocabulary line

fixes.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].
fixes.why: 'importance', 'valued', 'sector' are plain; marked 'people-facing', 'solitary', 'across virtually every sector'

fixes.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].
fixes.why: added the stronger phrase 'read social cues' in place of the weaker 'isolation'

fixes.answer: It has a profound effect. People with high emotional intelligence tend to have healthier, more fulfilling relationships because they can understand and respond to others' feelings [[sensitively]]. They handle disagreements calmly and communicate their own needs clearly. This creates an atmosphere of trust and [[mutual understanding]]. In essence, emotional intelligence is the quiet skill that makes relationships genuinely [[harmonious]].
fixes.why: 'understanding' alone is plain; marked the collocation 'mutual understanding'

fixes.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.
fixes.why: 'practice' and 'fixed' are plain; marked 'cultivated' and 'conscious effort'

fixes.answer: I strongly agree with this criticism. Traditional education has long [[prioritised]] exam results above all else, often neglecting the emotional and social skills that are equally vital for a fulfilling life. Skills like managing stress, empathising and collaborating are rarely taught explicitly. I think a more [[holistic]] education, one that develops the whole person, would produce far more [[well-rounded]] and capable adults.
